title: Mudflats at low tide
paragraphs: Coastal mudflats look barren at low tide, yet they rank among the most productive habitats on Earth. Each tidal cycle delivers a fresh load of nutrients, which fuels dense populations of microscopic algae in the upper layer of sediment. These algae feed snails, worms and small crustaceans, and those animals in turn sustain flocks of migratory shorebirds that cross whole continents to feed there. Some ecologists once assumed that the birds merely exploited a resource that would have flourished without them. Recent field experiments suggest otherwise: where birds were kept out by netting, the sediment became compacted and the algae thinned, implying that the birds' probing and trampling help keep the system healthy. If this interpretation holds, protecting the flats means protecting the birds as well.
